comments.text: In Brazil, we are currently dealing with a similar case. Three nursing technicians (one administering the injections and two covering it up) are accused of killing at least three people in a private hospital’s ICU, with more deaths still under investigation. They injected potassium chloride using forged prescriptions and watched as the victims' hearts stopped. They would only perform CPR if someone was nearby to avoid suspicion, but then they would simply try to kill the patient again later. In one case, they even injected cleaning products. They were only caught because the hospital has an internal protocol to analyze every death; they found it suspicious that patients who were actually improving were dying. They reviewed the security footage and discovered the truth. The hospital didn't hide anything or try to cover it up.

comments.text: I knew someone that I suspected of being an AOD. She was a friend of a friend that I met at a party. She later started dating another friend of mine so I saw her a few times. She laughed about running over an ex with a car, but pressured him into dropping charges by threatening his parents. Then she talked about how much she loved her job because she abused the patients but they couldn't fight back because they were sick and elderly. I called the hospital she worked at and told HR. As in the video she got fired but did not lose her credentials. She immediately got a job in a neighboring city and started a supply closet affair with a married doctor. transcript: What's worse, a nurse who is also a secret serial killer or the hospital that tries to cover it all up? This is the twisted murderous story of Charles Cullen, New Jerseyy's own angel of death and the hospitals that thought nobody would notice. Charles Cullen was born and raised in Northern New Jersey. And right off the bat, things didn't go well for him. As a young child, he lost his father and then his mother before he was even out of high school. These traumas left deep psychological scars that only worsened because of bullying and isolation. Charles knew he needed structure in his life, so he enlisted in the Navy and spent years living under the ocean in a nuclear submarine. Unfortunately, the bullying did not stop. You see, Charles was different. He was weird. He was depressed, socially awkward, and increasingly turned to alcohol, which only worsened his behavior and isolation. One time in the Navy, he went ashore and drank so much that he passed out under the hot sun barefoot. When he woke up hours later, his feet were burnt to a crisp. His superior showed him no sympathy either, forcing him to work in a pair of shoes too small for his feet and only giving him mild painkillers. [music] Charles was a laughingstock. Ultimately, he didn't fit in well with his bosses who were always looking over his shoulder. He needed a job with less oversight, like a night nurse in the ICU. So, Charles was discharged from the Navy and decided to enroll in nursing school. Despite his bizarre personality, he maintained steady work, got married, even had two children. And while on the surface, things appeared normal. Behind closed doors at the hospital, Charles was killing people left and right. His murders weren't all exactly the same, but they usually followed a pattern. He often worked night shifts in the intensive care unit treating burn victims and other seriously ill patients when they were short staffed and no visitors were present. To begin, he would identify a victim, a 72-year-old judge, a 21-year-old college student. Here, Charles did not discriminate and often killed randomly. So, just by being his patient, your life was instantly in danger. Then, Charles would head to the Pixus machine, a computerized drug dispenser, to get a dose of a drug called Dejoxin. In normal doses, it can help control the rhythm of the heart. In an overdose, it can trigger lethal heart arrhythmias. It was also a drug that was not routinely tested for in autopsies, meaning that there was a good chance nobody would even notice it in a patient's system. Then, while patients slept in their beds and other night shift nurses were out of the room, Charles would either inject the medication into a patient directly or tamper with their IV saline [music] bag. He murdered patients like this over a career that spanned 15 plus years. But why did it take so long for him to get caught? This is where things get really dark. Because so many of Charles's victims were already in the ICU, their deaths weren't often very suspicious. They were on the brink of death anyway, so nobody suspected any foul play. Also, Charles was clever in how he got hold of the Dejoxin. He took advantage of the flawed Pixus machines, entering the code for Tylenol that happened to share the same drawer. Or he would enter the code for Dejoxin, cancel the order immediately, and the drawer would open anyway. These workarounds created a confusing paper trail. Lots of canceled orders and odd Pixus activity, but little direct proof that he'd actually given the drug to patients. But more importantly, while it did take over a decade to put Charles behind bars, that's not because he never got caught. In fact, he got caught over and over again. He just didn't get punished. On numerous occasions, a hospital where Charles worked would find the circumstances of a patient's death unusual, and they would begin a quiet sort of inquiry. Charles was repeatedly implicated in these investigations, but his bosses could never quite prove it. So, what did the hospitals do? Well, they could call the police, begin a proper criminal investigation, and open themselves to a liability and PR nightmare. They'd hired a serial killer to care for patients. Not exactly a ringing endorsement to visit for your next checkup. So, these hospitals did what now seems unthinkable. They made Charles a deal. If he resigned, they'd end their investigation and give him neutral references. This left Charles without a job, but with an active nursing license and a spotless record. He ultimately worked at about 10 hospitals, leaving a trail of death behind him as he kept getting more and more work. One time, Charles even received a phone call offering him a nursing position while he himself was being held in a psychiatric facility while having a mental breakdown. There was a nursing shortage. Charles happily worked grueling ICU night shifts. And it wouldn't be right to deny him a job for simply seeking mental health support, would it? So Charles kept working and kept killing. Up and down the New Jersey Turnpike he went, injecting recovering patients with dejoxin or insulin at whichever hospital would give him a look until it all came to an end at Somerset Medical Center. A cluster of patients started dying with bizarre lab results including unexplained spikes in insulin and dejoxin and that finally got someone's attention. An internal investigation went underway and after 3 months during which time Charles killed five more people. The authorities were finally called with a mountain of circumstantial evidence before them. Detectives picked up the phone and called around the state learning that similar deaths had occurred at other hospitals where Charles had worked. He had a police record, too, having been arrested years before for stalking a former coworker and breaking into her house. The detectives could tell Charles was their man, but they couldn't quite prove it. There were no eyewitnesses, no late night security camera footage. The hospitals that swept Charles's murders under the rug were panicking about legal ramifications, so they stonewalled detectives and rarely gave up legit evidence. Somerset Medical Center, the scene of the crime, made it particularly hard to investigate the case. They barred their staff from speaking to police unless their lawyer was present. They told police the Pixus machines only kept records for 30 days. It was only after detectives called the manufacturer that they learned this wasn't even true. Somerset either didn't know how the machines worked or they flat out lied. There was only one option. They needed a confession. Detectives enlisted nurse Amy, a coworker of Charles, to help bring him in. At first, Amy laughed off the idea that Charles was a murderer. He was a great nurse. He took shifts nobody else wanted and was one of her closest friends. Impossible, she said. Then they walked her through the entire story, showing her all the evidence they'd gathered so far. This made her nervous, so she contacted an old friend of hers that had worked with Charles years before. She corroborated the story, saying he was a creep and that she was surprised to learn that he was still nursing. Amy thought back on previous patients who had died. They were recovering. Then Charles took over and they died. My god, they were right. Charles was a murderer and it was up to her to bring him down. If Somerset found out she was secretly working with detectives, Amy believed she could lose her job and her health insurance, but she did it anyway. So Amy invited Charles out to lunch at a diner. Her heart was pounding through her chest as they sat down. Charles was all smiles. A lunchtime cheeseburger with his friend Amy. What could be better? The conversation started casually, friendly as always. Then she started to probe. All those patients who had died, what happened? Was someone responsible? Was it possible that Charles was capable of killing those people? Charles's friendly smile vanished. He stared at her with his cold, dead eyes. He tried to change the subject, but Amy kept pressuring. With tremendous pressure building up inside of him, he admitted it was possible he was capable of such a thing. And that was all the police needed to hear, who had been secretly listening through a wire Amy wore under her shirt. Charles stormed out of the restaurant, got in his car, and sped off. Amy had just stared into the eyes of a madman and brought him to justice. Police pulled Charles over and brought him in for questioning. What followed was a brutal 7-hour interrogation where he confessed to killing almost 40 people. Many suspect the actual number could be in the hundreds. But why did he do it? What could motivate someone to kill so many innocent people? Charles claimed that he wanted to end the suffering of his terminally ill patients. Unfortunately, [music] this didn't add up as not all of Charles's victims were terminally ill, and his actions caused many of them to suffer violent, painful deaths for days on end. He was not a righteous mercy killer. His true motives may never be known or simply might not even exist. Dozens of civil suits were filed against several of the hospitals where Cullen had worked, accusing them of negligent hiring, supervision, and failing to warn. Many of those cases were resolved through confidential settlements rather than full-on public trials. Charles is still alive, serving 18 consecutive life sentences at a state prison in New Jersey. But here's an ironic twist. After Charles was locked behind bars, he was contacted by a distant friend of a relative who is in desperate need of a kidney donation. Oddly enough, he was a perfect match. Charles Cullen, the angel of death, donated his kidney and helped save the young man's life. How about doctors who got caught on camera behaving very badly? Not to that degree, but click here to check that out. And as always, stay happy and healthy.
